vsm1.1:113.1: 113. As to the robe and the other requisites,
vsm1.1:113.2:
no hint, indication, roundabout talk, or intimation about robes and alms food
is allowable for a bhikkhu who is purifying his livelihood.
vsm1.1:113.3: But a hint, indication, or roundabout talk about a resting place is allowable for one who has not taken up the ascetic practices.
vsm1.1:114.1:
114. Herein, a “hint” is when one who is getting the preparing of the ground, etc., done for the purpose of making
a resting place is asked, “What is being done, venerable sir? Who is having it done?” and he replies, “No one”;
vsm1.1:114.2: or any other such giving of hints.
vsm1.1:114.3: An “indication” is saying, “Lay follower, where do you live?”—”In a mansion, venerable sir”—
vsm1.1:114.4: ”But, lay follower, a mansion is not allowed for bhikkhus.” Or any other such giving of indication.
vsm1.1:114.5: “Roundabout talk” is saying, “The resting place for the Community of Bhikkhus is crowded”; or any other such oblique talk.
vsm1.1:115.1: 115. All, however, is allowed in the case of medicine.
vsm1.1:115.2: But when the disease is cured, is it or is it not allowed to use the medicine obtained in this way?
vsm1.1:115.3: Herein, the Vinaya specialists say that the opening has been given by the Blessed One, therefore it is allowable.
vsm1.1:115.4: But the Suttanta specialists say that though there is no offence,
vsm1.1:115.5: nevertheless the livelihood is sullied, therefore it is not allowable.
vsm1.1:116.1:
116. But one who does not use hints, indications, roundabout talk, or intimation, though these are permitted by the Blessed
One, and who depends only on the special qualities of fewness of wishes, etc., and makes use only of requisites
obtained otherwise than by indication, etc., even when he thus risks his life,
vsm1.1:116.2: is called supreme in living in effacement,
vsm1.1:117.1:
117. It seems that the venerable one was cultivating seclusion at one time,
living in a certain forest with the Elder Mahā Moggallāna.
vsm1.1:117.2: One day an affliction of colic arose in him, causing him great pain.
vsm1.1:117.3: In the evening the Elder Mahā Moggallāna went to attend upon him. Seeing him lying down, he asked what the reason was.
vsm1.1:117.4: And then he asked, “What used to make you better formerly, friend?”
vsm1.1:117.5:
The elder said, “When I was a layman, friend, my mother used to mix ghee, honey,
sugar and so on, and give me rice gruel with pure milk. That used to make me better.”
vsm1.1:117.6: Then the other said, “So be it, friend. If either you or I have merit, perhaps tomorrow we shall get some.”
vsm1.1:118.1:
118. Now, a deity who dwelt in a tree at the end of the walk overheard their conversation.
Thinking “I will find rice gruel for the lord tomorrow,”
vsm1.1:118.2: he went meanwhile to the family who was supporting the elder and entered into the body of the eldest son, causing him discomfort.
vsm1.1:118.3:
Then he told the assembled relatives the price of the cure: “If you prepare rice gruel of such
a kind tomorrow for the elder, I will set this one free.”
vsm1.1:118.4:
They said: “Even without being told by you we regularly supply the elder’s
needs,” and on the following day they prepared rice gruel of the kind needed.
vsm1.1:119.1:
119. The Elder Mahā Moggallāna came in the morning and said, “Stay here, friend,
till I come back from the alms round.” Then he went into the village.
vsm1.1:119.2: Those people met him. They took his bowl, filled it with the stipulated kind of rice gruel, and gave it back to him.
vsm1.1:119.3: The elder made as though to go,
vsm1.1:119.4: but they said, “Eat, venerable sir, we shall give you more.” When the elder had eaten, they gave him another bowlful.
vsm1.1:119.5: The elder left. Bringing the alms food to the venerable Sāriputta, he said, “Here, friend Sāriputta, eat.”
vsm1.1:119.6: When the elder saw it, he thought, “The gruel is very nice. How was it got?”
vsm1.1:119.7: and seeing how it had been obtained, he said, “Friend, the alms food cannot be used.”
vsm1.1:120.1:
120. Instead of thinking, “He does not eat alms food brought by the likes of me,”
the other at once took the bowl by the rim and turned it over on one side.
vsm1.1:120.2: As the rice gruel fell on the ground the elder’s affliction vanished.
vsm1.1:120.3: From then on it did not appear again during forty-five years.
vsm1.1:121.1:
121. Then he said to the venerable Mahā Moggallāna, “Friend, even if one’s bowels come
out and trail on the ground, it is not fitting to eat gruel got by verbal intimation,”
vsm1.1:121.2:
and he uttered this exclamation: My livelihood might well be blamed If I were to consent to eat The honey and the gruel
obtained By influence of verbal hints. And even if my bowels obtrude And trail outside, and even though My
life is to be jeopardized, I will not blot my livelihood (Mil 370). For I will satisfy my heart By shunning
all wrong kinds of search; And never will I undertake The search the Buddhas have condemned.
vsm1.1:122.1: 122. And here too should be told the story of the Elder Mahā Tissa the Mango-eater who lived at Cīragumba (see §132 below).
vsm1.1:122.2:
So in all respects: A man who has gone forth in faith Should purify his livelihood And, seeing
clearly, give no thought To any search that is not good.
vsm1.1:123.1: 123. (d) And as livelihood purification is to be undertaken by means of energy,
vsm1.1:123.2: so virtue dependent on requisites is to be undertaken by means of understanding.
vsm1.1:123.3: For that is accomplished by understanding,
vsm1.1:123.4: because one who possesses understanding is able to see the advantages and the dangers in requisites.
vsm1.1:123.5:
So one should abandon greed for requisites and undertake that virtue by using requisites obtained
lawfully and properly, after reviewing them with understanding in the way aforesaid.
vsm1.1:124.1: 124. Herein, reviewing is of two kinds: at the time of receiving requisites and at the time of using them.
vsm1.1:124.2:
For use (paribhoga) is blameless in one who at the time of receiving robes, etc., reviews them either as mere
elements or as repulsive, and puts them aside for later use, and in one who reviews them thus at the time of using them.
vsm1.1:125.1: Here is an explanation to settle the matter.
vsm1.1:125.2: There are four kinds of use: use as theft, use as a debt?, use as an inheritance, use as a master.
vsm1.1:125.3:
Herein, use by one who is unvirtuous and makes use of requisites, even
sitting in the midst of the Community, is called “use as theft.”
vsm1.1:125.4: Use without reviewing by one who is virtuous is “use as a debt”;
vsm1.1:125.5: therefore the robe should be reviewed every time it is used, and the alms food lump by lump.
vsm1.1:125.6:
One who cannot do this should review it before the meal, after the meal, in the first
watch, in the middle watch, and in the last watch.
vsm1.1:125.7: If dawn breaks on him without his having reviewed it, he finds himself in the position of one who has used it as a debt.
vsm1.1:125.8: Also the resting place should be reviewed each time it is used.
vsm1.1:125.9: Recourse to mindfulness both in the accepting and the use of medicine is proper;
vsm1.1:125.10: but while this is so, though there is an offence for one who uses it without mindfulness after mindful acceptance,
vsm1.1:125.11: there is no offence for one who is mindful in using after accepting without mindfulness.
vsm1.1:126.1: 126. Purification is of four kinds: purification by the Teaching,
vsm1.1:126.2: purification by restraint, purification by search, and purification by reviewing.
vsm1.1:126.3: Herein, virtue of the Pātimokkha restraint is called “purification by the Teaching”;
vsm1.1:126.4: for that is so called because it purifies by means of teaching.
vsm1.1:126.5: Virtue of restraint of faculties is called “purification by restraint”;
vsm1.1:126.6: for that is so called because it purifies by means of the restraint in the mental resolution, “I shall not do so again.”
vsm1.1:126.7: Virtue of livelihood purification is called “purification by search”;
vsm1.1:126.8: for that is so called because search is purified in one who abandons wrong search and gets requisites lawfully and properly.
vsm1.1:126.9: Virtue dependent on requisites is called “purification by reviewing”;
vsm1.1:126.10: for that is so called because it purifies by the reviewing of the kind already described.
vsm1.1:126.11: Hence it was said above (§125): “There is no offence for one who is mindful in using after accepting without mindfulness.”
vsm1.1:127.1: 127. Use of the requisites by the seven kinds of trainers is called “use as an inheritance”;
vsm1.1:127.2: for they are the Buddha’s sons, therefore they make use of the requisites as the heirs of requisites belonging to their father.
vsm1.1:127.3: But how then, is it the Blessed One’s requisites or the laity’s requisites that are used?
vsm1.1:127.4: Although given by the laity, they actually belong to the Blessed One, because it is by the Blessed One that they are permitted.
vsm1.1:127.5: That is why it should be understood that the Blessed One’s requisites are used.
vsm1.1:127.6: The confirmation here is in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta (MN 3).
vsm1.1:127.7: Use by those whose cankers are destroyed is called “use as a master”;
vsm1.1:127.8: for they make use of them as masters because they have escaped the slavery of craving.
vsm1.1:128.1: 128. As regards these kinds of use, use as a master and use as an inheritance are allowable for all.
vsm1.1:128.2: Use as a debt is not allowable,
vsm1.1:128.3: to say nothing of use as theft.
vsm1.1:128.4: But this use of what is reviewed by one who is virtuous
vsm1.1:128.5: is use freed from debt because it is the opposite of use as a debt or is included in use as an inheritance too.
vsm1.1:128.6: For one possessed of virtue is called a trainer too because of possessing this training.
vsm1.1:129.1:
129. As regards these three kinds of use, since use as a master is best, when a bhikkhu undertakes virtue
dependent on requisites, he should aspire to that and use them after reviewing them in the way described.
vsm1.1:129.2:
And this is said: “The truly wise disciple Who listens to the Dhamma As taught by the Sublime One Makes use, after
reviewing, Of alms food, and of dwelling, And of a resting place, And also of the water For washing dirt from robes” (Sn 391).
“So like a drop of water Lying on leaves of lotus, A bhikkhu is unsullied By any of these matters, By alms
food, and by dwelling, And by a resting place, And also by the water For washing dirt from robes” (Sn 392).
vsm1.1:129.3:
“Since aid it is and timely Procured from another The right amount he reckons, Mindful without
remitting In chewing and in eating, In tasting food besides: He treats it as an ointment Applied upon a wound.” (Source untraced)
vsm1.1:129.4:
“So like the child’s flesh in the desert Like the greasing for the axle, He should eat
without delusion Nutriment to keep alive.” (Source untraced)
vsm1.1:130.1:
130. And in connection with the fulfilling of this virtue dependent on requisites there
should be told the story of the novice Saṅgharakkhita the Nephew.
vsm1.1:130.2: For he made use of requisites after reviewing,
vsm1.1:130.3:
according as it is said: “Seeing me eat a dish of rice Quite cold, my preceptor observed:
‘Novice, if you are not restrained, Be careful not to burn your tongue.’
vsm1.1:130.4:
On hearing my Preceptor’s words, I then and there felt urged to act And, sitting in a single
session, I reached the goal of Arahantship.
vsm1.1:130.5:
Since I am now waxed full in thought Like the full moon of the fifteenth (M III 277), And all
my cankers are destroyed, There is no more becoming now.”
vsm1.1:130.6: And so should any other man Aspiring to end suffering Make use of all the requisites Wisely after reviewing them.
vsm1.1:130.7: So virtue is of four kinds as “virtue of Pātimokkha restraint,” and so on.
